tldr: We propose Whole-Body Dexterity (WBD), a control framework for humanoids that uses the entire torso and arms as contact surfaces to hold and manipulate bulky objects around the body. The policy learned in simulation transfers zero-shot to a real Unitree G1, achieving a 90% task success rate while correcting coarse human teleoperation commands in real time.
hero_caption: The overall pipeline of Whole-Body Dexterity (WBD). It starts with generating a stable whole-body grasp dataset, pre-training reinforcement learning experts on spheres, warm-starting them to other shapes, and distilling them into a diffusion model based on proprioception and object geometry, finally deploying the policy to a real humanoid robot.
overview:
When humans carry a large cardboard box, we don't just pinch it with our fingertips. We press it firmly against our chest, wrap both arms around it, or tuck it under one arm to free up a hand to open a door. We skillfully use our entire body to hold and move objects. However, humanoid dexterous manipulation has so far remained largely confined to end-effectors or simple holding against the front of the body.

This paper focuses on a fresh perspective: "Can we treat the entire robot body as one giant multi-fingered hand?" If we view the torso as the "palm" and the arms as "fingers," we can scale up finger gaiting from multi-fingered hands to the whole body. Based on this idea, the authors built Whole-Body Dexterity (WBD), a general framework that uses any contact surface across the entire body to freely reposition objects around the torso.

Specifically, the pipeline first automatically generates millions of diverse whole-body grasps using energy-based optimization. Next, it trains reinforcement learning experts (WBD-EX) to transition between these grasps and distills the resulting trajectory data into a diffusion-based controller that takes only proprioception and object geometry features as input. This controller receives coarse teleoperation commands from a human and corrects them in real time into joint commands that maintain contact without dropping the object.

In experiments on a real Unitree G1 humanoid, the robot achieved zero-shot transfer for a series of whole-body manipulation tasks. It repositioned basketballs and boxes onto its shoulder, stowed them under its arm, and completed a long-horizon task: picking a box from a shelf, stowing it under one arm, walking to carry it to a table, and placing it down. While direct teleoperation retargeting succeeded in only 18% of trials and a generalist whole-body controller managed just 4%, the proposed method achieved an impressive 90% success rate on these challenging tasks.
contributions: Establishing a pipeline that treats the torso and appendages as contact surfaces to automatically generate and verify mode-constrained (left arm, right arm, bimanual) stable whole-body grasp candidates.
Developing WBD-EX, a mode-constrained regrasping reinforcement learning expert that hands over objects between arms while sliding and rolling whole-body contacts.

Realizing a distilled diffusion controller that corrects coarse teleoperation commands into safe contact behaviors using only proprioception and a 5D object geometry descriptor without privileged object states.

Demonstrating zero-shot transfer on a real Unitree G1 humanoid, achieving a 90% success rate across tasks including repositioning basketballs and boxes around the torso and long-horizon shelf-to-table carrying with locomotion.

sections.heading: Turning the Robot's Entire Body into a Hand: The Concept of Whole-Body Dexterity
sections.summary: The authors propose whole-body dexterity, using not just end-effectors but the entire arms and torso as contact surfaces to manipulate objects like humans do. Expanding multi-fingered hand regrasping to the whole body enables dynamic object repositioning with rolling and sliding contacts under the constraints of two arms and a torso.
sections.details:
When carrying heavy loads, humans brace boxes against their chests or tuck them under one arm to free up the other hand. The authors define this ability to treat the limbs and torso as a single, highly dexterous manipulator as "Whole-Body Dexterous Manipulation."

While the term "whole-body coordination" has been used in humanoid research, it has mostly referred to legs and hips coordinating to position end-effectors, or statically pressing a box against the front of the body. There was no general framework for dynamically moving an object across various regions of the body while making and breaking contact with arbitrary links.

This is where an analogy to multi-fingered hands becomes useful. If we view the torso as the "palm" and the arms as "fingers," the robot should be able to manipulate objects with its whole body just as a multi-fingered hand rotates an object. However, unlike hands with many fingers, a humanoid has only two arms. Releasing one arm requires the other arm to brace the object against the torso so it does not fall, which demands complex control involving rolling and sliding across contact surfaces.

To address this, this work proposes Whole-Body Dexterity (WBD). The authors built a sim-to-real pipeline that first generates a massive dataset of whole-body grasps, trains reinforcement learning transition policies (WBD-EX) between them, and finally distills these experts into a single controller that runs without privileged information.

captions.F3: The whole-body grasp generation pipeline using energy-based optimization. Grasp poses are optimized across designated arm, torso, and leg contact candidate links. After simulation verification under increased gravity and disturbance wrenches, only stable grasps are stored in a voxelized dataset.

sections.heading: From Fingertip Dexterity to Whole-Body Manipulation
sections.summary: This section reviews related work across three contexts: whole-body contact manipulation, teleoperation, and contact sequencing. It highlights the unique approach of moving beyond static or planar contact planning to apply multi-fingered hand regrasping concepts to a whole-body humanoid.
sections.details:
The related work in this paper falls into three main categories:

- Whole-Body Manipulation: Early work explored whole-body manipulation with snake-like robots and using joint encoders as whole-body tactile sensors. Other studies have investigated hugging objects larger and heavier than end-effectors against the arms and chest, or using soft-torso robots. However, most of these methods were limited to frontal holding and did not offer a general way to reposition objects across diverse regions like the back or shoulders while maintaining an upright posture or walking.
- Teleoperation: Technologies that retarget human motions directly to humanoids in real time have advanced significantly. However, without force or tactile feedback, human operators cannot tell whether an object is securely braced or about to slip off. As a result, teleoperation has largely been confined to simple pick-and-place tasks using end-effectors.
- Dexterity as Contact Sequencing: In multi-fingered hands, "finger gaiting"—rotating an object by switching finger contacts—has been widely studied. The key novelty of this paper is elevating this principle of contact transitions (regrasping) from hands to a whole-body humanoid.

sections.heading: From Whole-Body Grasp Generation to RL Experts and Diffusion Distillation
sections.summary: The methodology consists of three main stages: first, automated generation of a whole-body grasp dataset via energy-based optimization; second, training reinforcement learning experts (WBD-EX) conditioned on target positions and grasp modes; and third, distilling them into a diffusion controller that corrects coarse human inputs using proprioception and geometric features.
sections.details:
### III-A Whole-Body Grasp Generation
First, a large set of stable whole-body grasp poses is generated from the robot's kinematic model and object meshes. Grasp modes are defined as left-arm grasp (L), bimanual grasp (B), and right-arm grasp (R). Because the torso of the Unitree G1 is very large, treating the whole torso as a single target leads to local minima. The authors split the torso surface into distinct regions and optimized grasps for each region independently, obtaining grasps distributed evenly across the body. Candidates are searched in parallel on the GPU by minimizing force-closure residual error using signed distance functions (SDF). Only grasps that survive strict simulation filtering—such as $4\times$ gravity and disturbance wrenches—are kept in the dataset.

### III-B Training WBD-EX
The resulting grasps are voxelized on a 2 cm grid to build a goal graph where each node is a combination of a voxel and a grasp mode. Transitions from one grasp to another are learned via reinforcement learning using PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization). A key feature is the constraint on mode transitions: direct transitions from L to R are forbidden, requiring the robot to pass through the bimanual mode B. In addition, single-arm goals require the other arm to be completely released. This enforces reliable handovers between arms. Furthermore, allowing a grace period of up to 0.48 seconds of temporary contact loss enables dynamic, momentum-driven regrasping rather than purely quasi-static bracing.

### III-C Distilling the WBD Controller
From the diverse repositioning trajectories generated by the experts, a deployable controller is learned without privileged information (such as true simulator object poses). The model uses a conditional diffusion model paired with an inverse kinematics network. The input consists solely of proprioceptive history (past joint angles and keypoint positions) and a 5D object geometry descriptor (sorted bounding box side lengths, log volume, and sphericity). At runtime, it takes coarse teleoperation commands from a human and uses gradient guidance to correct trajectories in real time into joint commands that maintain contact and prevent dropping.

captions.F2: The overall WBD pipeline. Stable grasps are voxelized into a dataset. WBD-EX experts pre-trained on spheres are warm-started to various object shapes. Trajectory data is then collected and distilled into a single diffusion model conditioned on object geometry features.

sections.heading: Correcting Coarse Teleoperation for Real Humanoid Whole-Body Manipulation
sections.summary: The approach was evaluated through simulation across 15 geometric primitives and on a real Unitree G1 humanoid. On the real robot, it performed shoulder and underarm repositioning of basketballs and boxes, as well as a long-horizon task involving picking from a shelf, stowing under an arm, walking, and placing on a table, achieving a 90% success rate that far outperforms baselines.
sections.details:
### IV-A & IV-B Simulation Evaluation
Training used 15 primitive shapes, including spheres, cubes, cuboids, and cylinders. In simulation, heavy noise was injected into expert outputs to mimic "clumsy human teleoperator commands," testing whether the WBD controller could correct them. Across paths visiting six body regions (front, left/right underarms, left/right shoulders, and back), the WBD controller recovered goal-reaching performance comparable to clean experts despite noisy inputs. It also demonstrated strong generalization to unseen shapes, extending time-to-failure on an unseen 180 mm sphere by 158% and an unseen 180 mm cube by 71%.

### IV-C Real-World Humanoid Experiments
Using a real Unitree G1, the system was evaluated under human teleoperation with an Xsens motion-capture suit. It was compared against direct joint retargeting (GMR) and SONIC, a whole-body teleoperation controller.

- Repositioning Around the Body: Using a size 3 basketball and a 15 cm cardboard box, the robot performed round-trip tasks: moving the object from the front to the shoulder ("shoulder tap"), stowing it under the arm ("underarm stow"), and returning it to the front. Direct GMR often dropped the object while moving the arms toward the target, resulting in low round-trip success (only 1/10 for box underarm stow). In contrast, WBD achieved a perfect 10/10 success rate.
- Long-Horizon Shelf Task: A complex sequence where the robot picks a box from a shelf, stows it under its left arm, walks upright to a table, retrieves it with both hands, and places it on the table. Both direct GMR and SONIC failed completely, dropping the box during walking or pose transitions. WBD withstood the walking disturbances and successfully carried the box.

Across all 50 real-world trials, direct GMR succeeded in only 18% (9/50) and SONIC in 4% (2/50), whereas the proposed WBD achieved an overwhelming 90% (45/50) success rate.

sections.heading: The Future and Challenges of Whole-Body Contact Manipulation
sections.summary: This work demonstrates the power of whole-body dexterity through a pipeline spanning large-scale grasp generation, reinforcement learning, and diffusion distillation. Future work will extend this framework to use leg and knee contact surfaces, enabling behaviors like resting heavy objects on a knee while shifting arm grasps.
sections.details:
This paper presented WBD, a systematic framework for whole-body dexterous manipulation that uses a humanoid's entire body as contact surfaces. By combining whole-body grasp enumeration, mode-constrained reinforcement learning regrasping, and diffusion distillation conditioned on proprioception and geometry, the system turns coarse human motion guidance into stable whole-body contact behaviors.

Notably, even though the lower body and pelvis were kept fixed during WBD-EX training, the distilled controller transferred seamlessly to the standing and walking real G1, proving robust against disturbances caused by locomotion.

Looking ahead, the authors highlight the integration of leg contacts. Leg grasps were excluded from expert training here to avoid complex coupling with walking and balance control. However, learning unified whole-body policies that include leg contacts could enable dynamic coordination commonly seen in humans, such as resting a very heavy box on a knee to support it while shifting arm grasps.

sections.heading: Appendix: Grasp Dataset Details, Training Tricks, and Diffusion Architecture
sections.summary: This section provides supplementary details on the grasp generation loss functions, voxelization, training efficiency via sphere warm-starting, escapability-based data filtering, and the conditional diffusion architecture.
sections.details:
Key engineering details that support the reproducibility and performance of this work include:

- Grasp Generation Optimization: The objective minimizes distances from candidate contact points on robot links to the object's SDF, force-closure residual ($E_{\text{closure}}$), and self-collision penalties between links. The torso mesh is tagged into sub-regions (chest, abdomen, back, and sides) to distribute contact points evenly across the body.
- Warm-Starting from Spheres: Training reinforcement learning from scratch on complex shapes like cuboids and cylinders often stalls. To address this, expert models were first trained for 15,000 iterations on symmetric, highly stable medium-to-large spheres. These weights then served as initialization (warm-start) for other shapes, reducing overall computational cost by about 20% while improving average goal completion across all routes, including the shoulders and back.
- Escapability Filtering: Even if a grasp is physically stable, the policy may struggle to transition away from it. The authors evaluated all 2.51 million generated grasps with a trained expert to measure the probability of successfully transitioning to other goals ("escapability"). Pruning grasps with low escapability significantly improved trajectory collection efficiency for distillation.
- Diffusion Architecture: The model uses a U-Net architecture. Inputs span 269 dimensions: 4 past steps (-15, -10, -5, 0 steps) of 24D arm keypoints, 14D joint angles, 14D target positions, and 14D tracking errors, combined with the 5D geometry descriptor. It predicts keypoint displacements for the next 2 steps (+5, +10 steps), which an inverse kinematics network converts into 14D joint command increments.

captions.F7: Sub-regions of the torso mesh used for grasp generation. Independent optimization for the right shoulder, back, left shoulder, right torso, front, and left torso ensures a well-distributed dataset without clustering on specific parts of the body.
captions.F8: The six goal regions in torso coordinates used for evaluating expert policies. The front and back require bimanual mode, while the underarms and shoulders require single-arm mode with the opposite arm fully released to count as reaching the goal.

takeaways: Viewing the torso as a palm and the arms as fingers provides an intuitive way to scale dexterous regrasping concepts from multi-fingered hands to whole-body humanoid manipulation.

In teleoperation with whole-body contacts, operators cannot feel contact states; shared autonomy via a diffusion model that interprets intent while automatically correcting contact is highly effective.
Pre-training reinforcement learning on symmetric spheres and warm-starting to other shapes drastically cuts the computational cost of learning contact-rich whole-body tasks.
Static stability in simulation does not guarantee successful dynamic transitions, making escapability-based filtering essential for building practical whole-body grasp datasets.
limitations: Leg contacts were excluded from WBD-EX training, leaving lower-body motions to standing and walking controllers; true whole-body manipulation involving the legs, such as resting a load on a knee to regrasp, has not yet been achieved.
Using a simple 5D bounding-box descriptor for object geometry limits applicability to objects with extreme indentations or complex everyday items with handles.
Real-world teleoperation experiments were conducted with a single experienced operator who trained for over 8 hours; performance when guided by untrained operators remains unverified.
